$comment: burgee's capability matrix against commander, yargs and meow, with the evidence for every cell. Rendered by <CapabilityMatrix pkg="burgee" />; scripts/capabilities-lock.test.ts holds every cell to its test, grade or source.

rows.why: Every command answers `--json` with one `{ ok, data }` or `{ ok, error }` document on stdout, from the same declaration as its text output.

ours.title: serves --json from the same declaration, with the envelope

meow.note: meow returns the parsed flags to the program; it writes no output format of its own.

rows.why: Any program prints its commands, arguments, options, choices, defaults and effects as JSON, without running a handler.

ours.title: is the manifest as data: name, version, commands with arguments

rows.why: Any program serves its commands as MCP tools over stdio, so an agent can call them without a wrapper.

ours.title: completes the handshake and names the program

rows.why: A program run by a coding agent knows which agent it is and turns interaction off, even when a terminal is attached.

ours.title: names the agent from the environment and turns interaction off

commander.note: No agent variable is read anywhere in the installed package.

yargs.note: No agent variable is read anywhere in the installed package.

rows.why: Usage, config, auth, cancellation and runtime failures each exit with their own fixed code, so a script can branch on the code instead of the message.

commander.note: Every error commander raises, an unknown option included, exits 1; a program can pass its own code to error(), but there is no set of named codes.

yargs.note: Every failure yargs reports, usage or handler, exits 1.

meow.missing: only incorrect usage has its own code (2); there is none for config, auth or cancellation

rows.capability: Completions for bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell
rows.why: Every program prints a completion script for each of the four shells, generated from the same declaration as its help.

yargs.missing: bash and zsh only; no fish or PowerShell script

rows.why: A cleanup a command registered runs when the user presses Ctrl+C, and the process then ends by the signal, which a shell reports as 130.

ours.title: runs the handler the program registered before the process goes

commander.note: commander's only signal listeners forward the signal to an executable subcommand's child process.

yargs.note: No signal is handled anywhere in the installed package.

meow.note: meow parses and returns; it runs no command, so there is nothing of its own to clean up.

rows.capability: No help screen on a runtime error
rows.why: A command that fails prints its error, not the usage text, so the message is not buried under help it did not ask for.

ours.title: leaves with the declared code and renders the message, hint and fix

commander.note: Help after an error is opt-in and covers commander's own usage errors; an action's error is not caught at all and escapes with its stack.

yargs.missing: a rejected handler prints the help screen by default; showHelpOnFail(false) stops that only by stopping it for usage errors too

meow.note: meow parses and returns; it runs no command, so a runtime error never passes through it.

rows.capability: Config, env and flag layers with the winning source named
rows.why: Values resolve flag over env over config file over package.json over default, and `config explain` or `--explain <option>` says which layer won.

ours.title: then each option and the source that won

commander.missing: reads no config file; a program loads one itself and sets each value with the 'config' source

yargs.missing: no record of which layer (flag, env, config) supplied a value

meow.note: meow reads package.json for the version and description only; it has no env or config-file layer.

rows.why: `--version` prints the version from the package.json that owns the entry file, unless the program declares its own.

ours.title: --version reads the package.json that owns the entry file

commander.note: The program passes the version string to .version() itself.

rows.why: `burgee/commander` runs commander's own tests at v15.0.0, unedited apart from the import, so a commander program keeps working after the import changes.

yargs.note: A different API; commander's suite does not apply to it.

meow.note: A different API; commander's suite does not apply to it.

rows.why: `burgee/yargs` runs yargs' own tests at v18.1.0, unedited apart from the import, so a yargs program keeps working after the import changes.

commander.note: A different API; yargs' suite does not apply to it.

yargs.note: its own suite; the oracle's control run is 802 / 804, because two usage tests read the version from the nearest package.json, which inside a vendored copy is not yargs'

meow.note: A different API; yargs' suite does not apply to it.

rows.why: `burgee/meow` runs meow's own tests at v14.1.0, unedited apart from the import, and the count it passes is published.

commander.note: A different API; meow's suite does not apply to it.

yargs.note: A different API; meow's suite does not apply to it.

meow.note: The oracle's control run is 146 / 148: one case imports meow's rollup build and one needs normalize-package-data, neither present in the vendored copy.
